title: Electron Shuttle Waiting Times for Electric Field Sensing
authors: Alberto Mayorgas, Alberto López-García, Enamul Haque, Javier Cerrillo
abstract: We explore the use of waiting-time statistics in a quantum electron shuttle for electric-field sensing. Electron shuttles convert nanomechanical motion into charge transport, showing a noise-broadened crossover between stochastic tunneling and mechanically assisted charge transfer. This allows investigation of how transport fluctuations encode electromechanical parameters. Using a single-level quantum shuttle in strong-Coulomb-blockade and high-bias regimes with a Markovian quantum master equation, we analyze stationary dynamics in phase space and waiting time distributions. By estimating the electromechanical coupling, proportional to the electric field, we evaluate the classical Fisher information in waiting times and compare it with the quantum Fisher information of the stationary state. We relate the metrological response to mean waiting time, variance, and Fano factor. Our results show that the crossover from tunneling to shuttling is characterized by enhanced fluctuations and increased parameter sensitivity, leading to a pronounced enhancement of the Fisher information.
summary: This paper investigates using the timing of electron tunneling events in a quantum electron shuttle to sense electric fields. By analyzing waiting-time statistics derived from a master equation model, the authors quantify the sensing limit by comparing classical and quantum Fisher information. The results highlight that the system's crossover regime offers superior sensitivity for electromechanical parameter estimation.
main_problem: The study aims to utilize waiting-time statistics from an electron shuttle system to estimate external electric fields, thereby quantifying the metrological potential of charge transport fluctuations.
main_result: The analysis shows that the crossover region between tunneling and shuttling regimes exhibits enhanced fluctuations and a pronounced enhancement in the Fisher information, improving parameter sensitivity for sensing.
method: The authors analyze stationary dynamics using Markovian quantum master equations to derive waiting time distributions (WTDs) and compare the resulting classical Fisher information against the theoretical quantum Fisher information.
model_or_system: The physical system is a quantum electron shuttle, modeled as a single-level quantum dot coupled to leads and an oscillating nanomechanical resonator. The dynamics are governed by a master equation incorporating tunneling, oscillator coupling ($\propto E$), and Ohmic dissipation.

main_assumptions: The dynamics are treated using a Markovian master equation derived via Born-Markov approximations, assuming constant parameters for frequencies and rates.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the electron shuttle setup. Figure 2 shows transitions in the Husimi function from Fock to toroidal shapes as coupling changes. Figure 3 displays WTD heatmaps showing frequency dependence on $\chi$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model and Hamiltonian, derives the master equation for the island-oscillator subsystem, analyzes stationary states via phase space methods, calculates WTDs, and finally applies quantum estimation theory to compare classical vs. quantum Fisher information.
why_interesting: This work bridges mesoscopic physics (quantum dots/shuttles) with quantum metrology by showing how temporal statistics (waiting times) in open quantum systems can be used as sensitive probes for external fields, a key area for AMO and quantum optics research.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Schematic representation of the electron shuttle. The central island (quantum dot) is modeled as a two-level system with level spacing εI (red) and moves in a harmonic potential with energy quantum ℏν, represented by the orange springs. The blue dash-dotted arrows indicate position-dependent electron tunnelling from the source to the island and from the island to the drain, with rates Γeˆx/λ and Γe−ˆx/λ, respectively, where ˆx is the island displacement and λ is the tunnelling length. The applied bias V controls the island–oscillator coupling strength χ, while the gray dashed arrow denotes mechanical damping at rate κ due to the coupling of the oscillator to a thermal bath.

FIG. 2: Husimi function of the stationary solution in the electronic diagonal elements subspaces ρ(+) 0 = ⟨1| ρ0 |1⟩ (top row) and ρ(−) 0 = ⟨0| ρ0 |0⟩(bottom row), for three values of the electric field χ = 0.1ν, 0.35ν, 0.6ν in the tunneling, crossover and shuttle regimes respectively (left to right columns). The axis represent the real and imaginary part of the phase space parameter α. The parameters used are Γ = 0.01ν, κ = 0.05ν, λ = 2x0 and an oscillator basis of size N = 50.

FIG. 4: Mean waiting time (solid blue) and standard deviation (dashed) in ν−1 units at the left axis, and Fano factor (orange) at the right axis. Magnitudes are derived from the waiting time distribution of the electron shuttle (7). The parameters used are Γ = 0.01ν, κ = 0.05ν, λ = 2x0 and an oscillator basis of size N = 50. The WTD has been calculated in a 1000 elements time window of τ ∈[0, 300ν−1].

FIG. 3: Heatmap of the waiting time distribution w(τ) as a function of the coupling χ (in ν units) and the waiting times (in ν−1 units). The WTD has been calculated in a 1000 elements time window of τ ∈[0, 300ν−1], in logarithmic scale to increase the point density for low waiting times. The horizontal dashed line identifies the period of the oscillator in the shuttle regime, 2π/ν ≃6.28ν−1. The parameters used are Γ = 0.01ν, κ = 0.05ν, λ = 2x0 and an oscillator basis of size N = 50.

FIG. 6: Quantum Fisher Information for a continuous measurement (11) divided by the measuring time T (blue), and QFI divided by the CFI of Figure 5 bottom panel (orange), both as function of the coupling χ. The parameters used are Γ = 0.01ν, κ = 0.05ν, λ = 2x0 and an oscillator basis of size N = 50.
